title: How Soap Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how soap works, starting with a book pre-order plug and a shout-out to Dr. Bronner's. They cover soap's basic ingredients (fat or oil plus an alkali such as lye), the chemistry of why oil and water don't mix, how soap molecules' hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails surround grime and lift it away, and how soap can break apart lipid-membrane viruses such as the coronavirus. They then trace soap history from ancient Mesopotamia and Rome (including the mythical Mount Sapo legend) through Crusader-era Aleppo soap, Castile soap, and 19th-century brands like Ivory and Palmolive. They discuss liquid soap, Irish Spring, handwashing guidelines, the FDA ban on triclosan and triclocarban in antibacterial soap, bar soap hygiene, and the shift from soap to synthetic detergents like Dreft and Tide. The episode closes with handwashing advice and a listener mail correction about yearling livestock in the Billy the Kid episode.

segments.title: Book pre-order plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts promote the Stuff You Should Know book pre-order with a poster gift, then open with banter about soap, a shout-out to Dr. Bronner's, and Chuck's wife Emily making soap.

segments.title: Soap ingredients and oil-water chemistry
segments.summary: Soap is a fat or oil combined with an alkali such as lye made from wood ash. The hosts explain why oil and water don't mix, surface tension, and how soap molecules have hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends and act as surfactants.

segments.title: How soap lifts grime and kills viruses
segments.summary: Soap molecules surround grease and dirt in micelles and lift it off skin to be rinsed away. Soap can also tear apart lipid-membrane viruses, including the coronavirus, and the hosts contrast this with alcohol-based sanitizer.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break taken after the discussion of soap and handwashing.

segments.title: Ancient soap history and Mount Sapo legend
segments.summary: Soap-making in Mesopotamia and saponification. The hosts discuss the mythical Mount Sapo legend, Roman soap use for cleaning and hair, and that the Elder Pliny mentioned soap.

segments.title: Crusaders, Aleppo soap, and Castile soap in Europe
segments.summary: Soap-making guilds in Europe, the story of Crusaders bringing Aleppo soap back from Syria, and the rise of Castile soap made from olive oil, along with observations on liquid soap texture.

segments.title: Soap in America: Ivory, Palmolive, Life Boy, liquid soap
segments.summary: Soap use spreading in the US after the Civil War, Ivory soap's floating origin story, Palmolive's name, Life Boy and body odor marketing, and the Minnetonka Corporation's soft soap pump buyout.

segments.title: Irish Spring origins
segments.summary: Irish Spring's scent, reportedly developed in Germany in 1970 and sold in the US from 1972, with its German name joked about.

segments.title: Handwashing guidelines and antibacterial soap ban
segments.summary: How to wash hands, the CDC's first handwashing guidelines for hospitals in the 1980s, the FDA ban on triclosan and triclocarban in antibacterial soap, and a 1965 study showing bar soap does not transmit bacteria.

segments.title: Soap versus detergent and the rise of Tide and Dreft
segments.summary: Detergents are synthetic soaps that avoid soap scum in hard water. Procter and Gamble's Dreft and later Tide are discussed, along with Tide's water-mineral testing, and the environmental harm of detergents to fish.

segments.title: Wrap-up and handwashing reminder
segments.summary: Hosts sum up the episode and encourage frequent handwashing.

segments.title: Listener mail: yearling correction
segments.summary: A listener from Wyoming corrects the earlier Billy the Kid episode, explaining that yearling refers to livestock about a year old, and the hosts discuss the book The Yearling.
